# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
# Review of "Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations"

This is a strong follow-up. It addresses most of the open questions from the earlier papers:
- **Decay:** it tests persistence with randomised data over two years.
- **Unrecorded work:** it adds a second hours measure taken from system logs.
- **Meetings:** it registers the mediation test before the 24-month outcomes existed.
- **Meta-analysis claim:** it shows the meta-analysis's four "long follow-up" studies were all uncontrolled and used scheduled hours, which settles the concern I raised about that paper.
- **Re-analysis claim:** it answers "entirely an artifact" with the standard the re-analysis itself recommended.

The core result is credible: a randomised two-year gain of about 8–10% per hour, smaller than at nine months. Its weak points are four:
- The log-hours measure is never defined clearly enough to support the "stricter" label.
- The mediation is overstated as confirmation.
- Two figures don't reconcile.
- The Summary frames some results more favourably than the body text does.

**Arithmetic checks.** The main figures reproduce:

| Figure | Calculation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Varden output per hour, timesheets | 0.966 / 0.88 | +9.8% |
| Varden output per hour, logs | 0.966 / 0.89 | +8.5% |
| Halden hours change | 34.9 / 40.3 | −13.4% |
| Halden output per hour | 96.8 / 0.866 | +11.8% |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 | 100% |

## 1. What do the system logs measure?

The paper calls log-in time on the case-management system the "stricter" hours measure. That label depends on what the logs capture.

**The logs probably miss some work.** They record time spent on cases inside the system. They probably exclude meetings, email, phone calls and anything done outside the system. So they are not a superset of timesheet hours. They catch unclaimed *case* work but miss unclaimed work of other kinds.

**The figures don't fit together if logs exclude meetings.**
- Treated offices cut recurring meetings by about 3.5 hours a week relative to control.
- Total timesheet hours fell by about 4.5 hours a week (12% of roughly 37.9).
- If logs exclude meetings, time on cases should have fallen by only about 1 hour, roughly 3%.
- The logs instead show an 11% fall, about 3.4 hours.

Either the logs count time while logged in during meetings (so "active" needs defining), or the hours and meetings figures are inconsistent.

**It matters for the mediation analysis.** The outcome there is output per log-measured hour. If meeting time isn't in the denominator, cutting meetings can't raise that outcome simply by removing meeting hours. It would have to work through something else, such as better concentration. That would change how the 47% should be read.

## 2. The mediation analysis is overstated

**"Confirms" is too strong.** Mediation estimates rest on the assumption, which the Limitations admit, that nothing unmeasured influences both the mediators and the outcome. Also, the meetings hypothesis came from these same seven treated offices, and the test was registered after nine months of their data had been seen. A registered test on the data that generated a hypothesis is better than an unregistered one, but it is not independent replication. "Is consistent with" or "supports" fits the evidence.

**The confidence intervals look too narrow.** The paper credits "a larger sample of office-months." But office-months within an office are not independent, so the effective sample size is still 14 offices. A 95% CI of 28–66% for an indirect-effect share estimated from 7 v 7 offices looks narrow. Please state how the clustering was handled and report office-level bootstrap intervals.

**The two mediators are likely related.** Fewer meetings plausibly reduce fatigue. How the shared variance is divided between the pathways should be stated, and the shares should be shown under different orderings.

**Timing of measurement.** If the mediators and output are measured over the same period, the meetings share may partly reflect reverse causation. For example, offices that were coping better may have cancelled meetings more readily.

## 3. Figures and design problems around meetings

**Where did the baseline meeting data come from?** The nine-month report said meeting data were collected in month six only. This report gives baselines of 7.4 hours (treated) and 7.2 hours (control). If calendars were extracted retrospectively, say so and describe how complete they are.

**The control-office average doesn't reconcile.**
- Two control offices cut meetings to 5.0 hours a week at month 15.
- If the other five stayed near 7.2 hours, the control mean would be about 6.6 hours: (5 × 7.2 + 2 × 5.0) / 7.
- The paper reports 7.0 hours.

Either the other control offices increased their meeting time, or a figure is wrong. Please give office-level values.

**The meeting audit contaminated the control group.** Two of seven control offices adopted part of the mechanism being tested. That likely biases the 24-month difference-in-differences estimate *downward*, and the mediation estimate too. The paper should:
- note this as a threat to the comparison;
- report a sensitivity analysis excluding those two offices, or estimating their post-audit months separately.

The audit itself is honestly caveated. Its 4.1% figure is a before–after comparison and also open to regression to the mean.

## 4. The Summary mixes measures and softens the Halden reversions

**The decline is reported across two different measures.** The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months." The 12.5% used timesheets; the 8.5% used logs. The like-for-like change is 12.5% to 9.8%, as section 3 correctly says. The Summary should lead with that comparison.

**The decline hasn't been tested.** The nine-month CI (6.9 to 18.4) and the 24-month CI (4.6 to 15.2) overlap heavily. "Consistent with some fading" is fair, but report a test of the change itself.

**When is "24 months" measured?** If the 24-month estimate averages over the whole two years, the effect at the end of the period may be lower than 9.8%. If it covers only the final months, say so.

**The Halden reversions are framed too broadly.** The Summary says all three "had client-facing or coverage obligations." But the marketing agency cited client deadlines. That is deadline-driven work, which the meta-analysis would code as *discretionary*. So it is a reversion within the work type where reduced hours are claimed to work, which matters for the sector conclusions. The Summary should report it as such.

## 5. The Halden subset

**Non-response.** Only 14 of the 23 organisations agreed to provide data. Organisations that are struggling or have reverted may be less likely to reply. Compare the 14 with the 9 non-responders on their pilot-era characteristics.

**"Upper bound" is too strong.** There is no comparison group, and conditions over two years could have moved output either way. "Likely optimistic" is more accurate than a strict upper bound.

**Missing details.**
- Confirm that all 11 continuing organisations have time tracking. Only 17 of the 23 had both records and time tracking during the pilot.
- Comparing against a baseline more than two years old picks up unrelated changes over that period.

## 6. Smaller points

- **Observation effects.** Two years of data argues against short-lived novelty. But it doesn't rule out effects of being observed, which persist for as long as evaluation does. Control offices were also observed, which helps, but say this explicitly when answering the re-analysis.
- **Counter-arm costs.** The figures of 12% more staff and a 9% rise in cost per contact are the county's own estimates. Give the method, since this is the paper's only cost figure. It is also the first cost evidence in the series, and it should be in the Summary.
- **Earlier points still open.** The schedule format, and with it whether the sick-day fall is partly due to fewer working days, is still not reported. Resignations still have no CI.
- **Conflict of interest.** The authors include the original Halden author and the Varden authors who proposed the meetings hypothesis. They are judging critiques of their own work, so a short disclosure statement would help.

## Bottom line

The main conclusions stand:
- A randomised, two-year gain in output per hour of roughly 8.5–9.8% in discretionary work.
- Some fading from nine months, of uncertain size.
- Output per employee slightly below control.
- Coverage-bound work abandoned for clear reasons.

The responses in section 5 are fair to both the re-analysis and the meta-analysis. Before publication, the authors should:
1. Define what the logs measure and reconcile them with the meetings figures.
2. Present the mediation as supportive rather than confirmatory, with intervals that account for clustering.
3. Reconcile the control-office meeting mean, and address the contamination from the meeting audit.
4. Use the like-for-like decline in the Summary, and describe the marketing-agency reversion accurately.

On the open question from the earlier papers, the gain persists at two years in one public employer, at about two-thirds to three-quarters of its nine-month size. Whether cutting meetings without cutting hours could deliver most of the gain is now the most important untested question.
